item.title: Alamogordo Invited to Welcome Home Veteran Larry Sanmann From Honor Flight
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — Alamogordo is invited — and challenged — to fill VFW Post 7686 on Saturday night and welcome home Air Force veteran Larry Sanmann as he returns from Washington, D.C., with Rio Grande Honor Flight Mission 22.

The homecoming, hosted by the U.S. Veterans Motorcycle Club, Trinity Chapter, with the Patriot Guard Riders, begins at 7 p.m. Organizers are asking the public to bring American flags, welcome home banners and all the patriotism they can carry, giving Sanmann the hometown welcome many Vietnam veterans never received.

It is a fitting salute to a man whose working life was measured in turbine blades and the roar of jet engines. From the flight lines of Vietnam to the hangars at Holloman Air Force Base, Sanmann spent more than three decades keeping some of America's most storied aircraft in the air.

From Nebraska to Vietnam

Sanmann enlisted in the Air Force in 1967 from his hometown of McCool Junction, Nebraska, and trained as a jet engine mechanic. His first assignment was Cannon Air Force Base in Clovis, but his stay in eastern New Mexico was a short one.

Before long he was at Phan Rang Air Base in South Vietnam, where he served from 1968 to 1969. There he maintained the jet engines of the F-100 Super Sabre, the fighter-bomber that flew close air support missions throughout the war.

Engines around the world

After Vietnam, Sanmann was assigned to Tinker Air Force Base in Oklahoma, where most of the Air Force's jet engines went for depot-level overhaul and maintenance. There he worked on just about every jet engine the service was flying at the time.

His next stop was McConnell Air Force Base in Kansas, working on the Pratt & Whitney J57 engines of the KC-135 Stratotanker, the workhorse of aerial refueling and cargo airlift. From McConnell he deployed to Andersen Air Force Base on Guam in 1972 in support of Operation Bullet Shot, the massive buildup of B-52 Stratofortress bombers in the Pacific during the Vietnam War. On Guam he kept the B-52s' engines running.

Sanmann then moved to Kadena Air Base in Okinawa, Japan, where he continued maintaining KC-135 engines. From there he was stationed at Hill Air Force Base in Utah, working on the engines of the F-4 Phantom II and the F-16 Fighting Falcon.

Home at Holloman

His final Air Force assignment brought him back to New Mexico, to Holloman Air Force Base, where he closed out his career working on the F-15 Eagle. Sanmann retired after 21 years of active duty at the rank of master sergeant (E-7).

Retirement didn't last long. As Sanmann tells it, he simply walked across the flight line and took a job with DynCorp maintaining T-38 Talons — and, once again, their jet engines. He later worked on the German Air Force's F-4 Phantoms and their engines at Holloman until 2004, when he retired a second time, "so he says."

To keep from getting bored, he then drove the shuttle between Alamogordo and Holloman. Today Sanmann is fully retired and makes his permanent home in Alamogordo.

This weekend he will travel with Honor Flight Mission 22 to Washington, D.C., organized by Rio Grande Honor Flight, to visit the memorials built in honor of those who served. After a lifetime spent keeping America's aircraft flying, he says he is looking forward to it.

If you go

Join the welcome home celebration for Larry Sanmann:

• When: Saturday, Sept. 26, 2026, at 7 p.m.• Where: VFW Post 7686, 700 Highway 70 West, Alamogordo• Hosted by: U.S. Veterans Motorcycle Club, Trinity Chapter, with the Patriot Guard Riders and Rio Grande Honor Flight

Bring your flags, your banners and a friend. Sanmann gave 21 years in uniform and decades more on the flight line — it takes one evening to tell him thank you.

item.title: Lady Tigers Outlast Ruidoso in Five-Set Thriller
item.description:
Alamogordo closes the match on an 8-0 run to beat Ruidoso; Tularosa falls to Quemado.

It took all five sets and every ounce of energy the Lady Tigers had, but Alamogordo pulled away from Ruidoso when it mattered most, winning 27-25, 14-25, 25-15, 24-26, 15-6.

The win improves Alamogordo to 5-7 on the season.

The opening set set the tone. Neither team could pull away, and it took extra points before Alamogordo finally closed it out 27-25.

The Lady Tigers looked ready to build on that momentum early in the second set, jumping out to a 9-4 lead. Ruidoso answered emphatically. The Warriors took a 12-11 lead, stretched it to 18-12 and outscored Alamogordo 21-5 after trailing 9-4 to win the set 25-14 and even the match at 1-1.

Alamogordo responded with its most dominant set of the night. The Lady Tigers led 8-3, then 15-5 and 19-11 before cruising to a 25-15 win and a 2-1 match lead.

The fourth set looked headed the same direction. Alamogordo led 10-5 and still held a 15-13 edge midway through, but Ruidoso rallied to take a 23-20 lead. The Lady Tigers fought back to force extra points, but Ruidoso escaped 26-24 to tie the match 2-2 and force a deciding fifth set.

With the match on the line, Alamogordo took control early, scoring the first three points of the fifth set. Ruidoso clawed back within 7-6, but that was as close as the Warriors would get. The Lady Tigers scored the final eight points of the match to win the set 15-6 and seal the victory.

Alamogordo is back in action Saturday at Socorro.

In other area action, Tularosa fell to Quemado in straight sets.

The loss drops the Lady Cats to 3-8 on the season. Tularosa returns home Tuesday to host Hatch Valley.

Alamogordo 3, Ruidoso 2 27-25, 14-25, 25-15, 24-26, 15-6 Record: Alamogordo 5-7. Next: at Socorro, Saturday.

Quemado 3, Tularosa 0 Record: Tularosa 3-8. Next: vs. Hatch Valley, Tuesday.

item.title: Tigers Rally Within Two, But Artesia Pulls Away for 54-19 Win
item.description:
Alamogordo NM- Artesia pulled away from Alamogordo on Friday, scoring 35 unanswered points after the Tigers cut the lead to two early in the third quarter, for a 54-19 win.

Artesia led 14-0 after the first quarter behind Logan Rodriguez, who threw a 62-yard touchdown pass to Layton Whitmire and ran for a 9-yard score. Alamogordo quarterback Nathanael Cereceres answered with a 14-yard touchdown run, and Russell's extra point made it 14-7. After Lucas Atkins hit Whitmire on a 4-yard touchdown pass, Cereceres found Aiden Rowe for a 31-yard score with 1:25 left in the half, sending the Tigers into halftime down 21-13.

Bryson Bloom opened the second half with a 67-yard touchdown run to pull Alamogordo within 21-19, but the two-point try to tie was no good. Artesia took over from there. Atkins threw touchdown passes of 35 yards to Kai Greathouse and 44 yards to Tyler Egeland, Rodriguez added a 40-yard run, Derek Ruiz returned an interception 30 yards for a score, and Chance Hocker tossed a 4-yard touchdown to Andres Ortiz to close out the scoring.

item.title: Public defender: Masked ICE grab at Otero County courthouse came moments after case was dismissed
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — Masked men who said they were ICE agents grabbed a man at the Otero County District Courthouse on Sept. 22, 2026 moments after a judge dismissed the criminal case he had come to court to fight, according to the top public defender for the 12th Judicial District. 

Dayna Louise Jones, the district's District Defender with the Law Office of the Public Defender, described the Sept. 22, 2026 incident in a Thursday email to the 12th Judicial District's Criminal Justice Coordinating Council. She wrote that people present told her office the detention "appeared to be coordinated and preplanned with local entities." 

"The courthouse should be a safe place for individuals who are seeing their cases through to their resolutions," Jones wrote.

"Abducted from the courthouse"

Jones wrote that the man, a client of her office, was "exercising his right to a jury trial" when he was taken immediately after his case was dismissed. His children, who were with him, described the men as wearing masks and traveling in an unmarked vehicle, according to the email.

The man has not been publicly identified. 

Jones acknowledged that she is not an immigration lawyer and said her aim was not to debate immigration policy. Her concern, she wrote, is the "chilling effect" on people who come to court because they are required to.

She pointed to Chaparral, a community near the border where she said many residents are undocumented. She wrote that she has interviewed alleged victims at the Chaparral fire station because they cannot pass the Border Patrol checkpoint to reach her office.

"Imagine if an alleged victim were taken from ICE immediately after their testimony in a jury trial," she wrote. Such a feeling, she added, "should not change because the person pictured is a defendant whose case has just been dismissed."

The man's family is "extremely upset, traumatized, and trying to figure out what happened to their loved one," Jones wrote. She asked council members to refer any immigration attorneys willing to help them.

State limits on sharing immigration status

Jones cited a 2025 state law on nondisclosure of sensitive personal information, which she said aims to keep state agency employees from disclosing a person's immigration status. 

She noted that the State Ethics Commission has sued New Mexico Probation and Parole under that law, in case D-101-CV-2025-02343. Jones wrote that she has no reason to believe Probation and Parole was involved in the Sept. 22 incident.

She did not say which local entities she believes coordinated with the agents. She wrote that regardless of whether any legal exceptions apply, a person who came to court "was deprived of his liberty immediately upon the actual criminal case against him being dismissed."

New Mexico has also restricted local cooperation with immigration enforcement more broadly. The Immigrant Safety Act, House Bill 9, signed by Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham in February, bars state and local public bodies from agreements with ICE for civil immigration detention. It took effect May 20.

Otero County's fight over ICE detention

The incident comes months after the state moved to cut Otero County's own ties to ICE. On April 1, Attorney General Raúl Torrez asked the New Mexico Supreme Court to void the county's agreement to hold ICE detainees at the Otero County Processing Center in Chaparral, which holds about 900 people at capacity.

The state argued the county lacks authority to detain people for civil immigration violations and never got required approval from the Department of Finance and Administration. County officials have defended the contract as a valid agreement. Ultimately the case was dropped by the AG office.

Chaparral is also the community Jones singled out in her email as home to many undocumented residents who are victims, witnesses and defendants in local cases.

Public Comment from Officials

A request for comment was sent Sunday to the office of Otero County Sheriff David Black and the County CEO, whose deputies provide courthouse security, asking whether the office knew of or assisted in the detention.

A request for comment was also sent Sunday to 12th Judicial District Judge Angie Schneider and the Court Clerk’s Office asking about the court's knowledge of the arrest and its policy on immigration enforcement at the courthouse. [

Jones closed her email by saying she believes no one on the council wants people "to be afraid to come to a criminal court proceeding only because of their nationality or origin."

item.title: Alamogordo Gives Vietnam Veteran Larry Sanmann a Hero's Welcome Home From Honor Flight
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — More than half a century after he came home from Vietnam, Larry Sanmann finally got the homecoming he deserved.

A police escort led the Air Force veteran to VFW Post 7686 on Saturday evening, where Mayor Sharon McDonald, District 51 state representative candidate Grace Nagamine, fellow veterans, family members and residents waited to welcome him home from Washington, D.C., with Rio Grande Honor Flight Mission 22. Flags and banners greeted Sanmann as he arrived at the post on Highway 70 West

The celebration was organized by the U.S. Veterans Motorcycle Club, Trinity Chapter, alongside the Patriot Guard Riders and Rio Grande Honor Flight. Organizers had asked the community to turn out in force and give Sanmann the kind of reception that many Vietnam veterans were denied when they returned from the war.

Mayor McDonald stated: "Larry Sanmann spent his life keeping America's aircraft in the air, and tonight Alamogordo got the chance to say thank you. Too many veterans came home to silence. We wanted Larry to come home to a welcome deserved."

Grace Nagamine a candidate for District 51 State Representative was on hand and said: "Seeing this community fill the VFW for Larry says everything about who we are here in southern New Mexico. We owe our veterans more than one night of cheers, but tonight was a good start, I was honored to be here to celebrate Larry and the veterans on hand tonight.”

Honor Flight programs fly veterans to the nation's capital at no cost to visit the memorials built in their honor. For Sanmann, the trip capped a career spent keeping American aircraft in the sky.

A native of McCool Junction, Nebraska, Sanmann joined the Air Force in 1967 and trained as a jet engine mechanic. After a brief first assignment at Cannon Air Force Base in Clovis, he was sent to Phan Rang Air Base in South Vietnam, where from 1968 to 1969 he maintained engines on the F-100 Super Sabre fighter-bombers flying close air support.

His career then carried him across the country and the Pacific. At Tinker Air Force Base in Oklahoma, the service's main engine overhaul depot, he worked on nearly every jet engine in the Air Force inventory. At McConnell Air Force Base in Kansas he maintained KC-135 Stratotanker engines, and in 1972 he deployed to Andersen Air Force Base on Guam for Operation Bullet Shot, keeping B-52 bombers running during the Vietnam War buildup. Assignments followed at Kadena Air Base in Okinawa, Japan, and Hill Air Force Base in Utah, where he worked on the F-4 Phantom II and F-16 Fighting Falcon.

He finished his military career at Holloman Air Force Base working on the F-15 Eagle, retiring as a master sergeant after 21 years of active duty. He didn't stay retired long. Sanmann went to work for DynCorp maintaining T-38 Talon engines, then worked on the German Air Force's F-4 Phantoms at Holloman until 2004. He later drove the shuttle between Alamogordo and Holloman before retiring for good.

Sanmann makes his home in Alamogordo, and on Saturday night, his hometown made sure he knew it he is a valued member of our community.

item.title: Independent Truckers and Teamsters: Now Is the Time for Action - A call to park it and roll slow, October 1–5, 2026
item.description:
Independent trucking interests and a vocal group within the teamsters has declared that enough is enough! A small but growing organic group of leaders in the trucking industry is calling out to independent media to get the word out to independent truckers and teamsters to park it and or roll slow, October 1–5, 2026 

America's truckers are hauling the nation's food at a loss, and Washington is looking the other way. Diesel has hit the highest prices ever recorded, families are paying more for everything on the shelf, and the President and Congress have offered drivers little more than talk. From October 1 through October 5, independent owner-operators and Teamsters must stand together, park their trucks, roll slow through the nation's cities, and demand that Washington act.

The crisis at the pump

Two years ago, in the week of September 23, 2024, the national diesel average was $3.54 a gallon. For the week of September 21, 2026, it reached $6.529, with the Midwest at $6.680, the East Coast at $6.268 and the West Coast at $7.456.

The cause is no mystery. The war with Iran has closed the Strait of Hormuz to a large share of oil and refined-product shipments for more than six months, while Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries have led Moscow to ban diesel exports. Drivers didn't start these wars, but they are paying for them at every fill-up.

What it costs to feed America

Take a refrigerated load of lettuce or strawberries leaving California's Central Valley. Two years ago, a run of about 2,200 miles from Fresno to Chicago cost a trucker roughly $1,520 in fuel. Today the same trip costs about $2,770, an increase of around $1,250. A 3,000-mile run from Fresno to New York has climbed from roughly $2,040 to about $3,700, an extra $1,660 on a single load. Fuel alone has gone from about 69 cents a mile to roughly $1.25.

For an owner-operator running 100,000 miles a year, that adds close to $50,000 in annual fuel costs. Many never see that money back, because most owner-operators with their own authority get freight through brokers on the spot market, where a separate fuel surcharge isn't necessarily paid. The driver fronts the cost of the diesel, and too often the rate doesn't cover it. In California, some truckers are filling up only enough for the day, hoping prices ease by their next shift.

For shoppers, the extra fuel on a coast-to-coast load works out to about 4 cents a pound of produce. For the trucker paying that bill up front, it's the difference between feeding a family and parking the truck for good.

We've won before

Truckers have been here before, and history shows what unity can do. In December 1973, a Kansas driver known on the CB as "River Rat" stopped his rig on Interstate 80 in Pennsylvania and sparked a movement that gave independent truckers their first national voice. In early 1974, as a nationwide shutdown spread, President Nixon froze diesel prices in an effort to end it.

When the Iranian Revolution triggered a second oil shock, about 75,000 truckers struck in 1979, calling for a diesel price freeze and subsidies for independent owner-operators. The protest lasted about a month, and fresh produce piled up in warehouses as picket lines slowed fuel terminals. It won a temporary mandatory fuel surcharge.

The lesson is plain: when truckers stand together, Washington moves. When we stand alone, we get picked off one load at a time.

Why independents and Teamsters must unite

Today's industry is more divided than it was in 1979. More than 350,000 truckers work as independent contractors, and only a small minority of drivers belong to a union. That division is exactly why unity matters now.

Independent owner-operators bring the numbers on the spot market and the freedom to park. The Teamsters, and the broader labor movement including the AFL-CIO, bring organization, political muscle and a voice in Washington. Together, drivers can make the case that record fuel costs aren't just a trucking problem. They are a crisis for every working family in America.

The call to action: October 1–5

Park it. Independent owner-operators, stay off the load boards and keep your trucks parked for five days. Let empty loading docks and quiet truck stops show what America looks like without us.

Roll slow. In major cities and on the beltways around the capitol, join slow-roll convoys that bring traffic to a crawl and put the fuel crisis in front of every commuter, reporter and lawmaker. Convoys keep moving. They leave a lane open for ambulances, fire trucks and police, and organizers notify local authorities ahead of time. The goal is to be impossible to ignore, never to trap a family on the way to the hospital.

Stand with us. Teamsters and AFL-CIO leaders, speak out publicly for these drivers, join the rallies, and press Congress on their behalf. Union members should check with their locals before any walkout, since many contracts contain no-strike clauses, but every member can show up, speak out and flood their representatives' phone lines.

Show up. Rally at state capitols, truck stops and congressional offices. Bring your fuel receipts. Bring your families. Tell your story.

Our demands to the President and Congress

Suspend the federal diesel tax until prices come down. Require a fuel surcharge that goes directly to the driver who buys the fuel, including on broker loads. Provide emergency relief for small trucking businesses and farmers crushed by fuel costs. And protect families facing higher prices for food, goods and heat this winter.

Discipline wins

This movement will be peaceful. No trucks stopped across lanes, no threats, no harassment of drivers who keep working. The violence that marred the 1970s strikes cost truckers public support and gave politicians an excuse to dismiss them. Today, one ugly video can erase a week of sacrifice. Our strength is our numbers, our discipline and the simple truth that nothing in this country moves without a truck.

Families are in crisis, and Washington is looking away. For five days, let's make sure they can't.

October 1–5. Park it. Roll slow. Stand together. Make them act.

item.title: In Memory of Margot Bratton
item.description:
Margot Bratton passed away on September 9, 2026, in El Paso, Texas, surrounded by family after a courageous four year battle with myasthenia gravis.

Born in Des Plaines, Illinois, Margot met John Bratton, the love of her life, on Bratton Lane in Round Rock, Texas, and they married in Georgetown, Texas. When the Air Force relocated John, their journey brought them to Alamogordo, New Mexico, where they continued their military adventures and eventually settled down. A beloved mother, grandmother, daughter, sister, coach, and proud military wife, she welcomed military children and families into her home, making it “that house on base” where everyone belonged.

As a track coach, Margot loved supporting her athletes and community. She enjoyed going to the movies, watching novelas, and listening to Taylor Swift and Selena. She especially loved hosting Sunday evening dinners, bringing friends and family together around her table. She dreamed of traveling across the United States in an RV, visiting New York City, and attending more Dallas Cowboys games.

She is survived by her husband, two sons, grandchildren, mother, and sister. Her love and generosity will live on in the lives she touched.

“He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty. I will say of the LORD, He is my refuge and my fortress: my God; in him will I trust.”
- Psalm 91:1-2 (KJV)

Services for Margot was be held at Scenic Chapel on Friday, September 25th with a visitation at 9:00 am followed by the funeral service at 10:00 am.

The Bratton family has entrusted their loved one to the care of Scenic Chapel to direct the funeral services.

item.title: Lincoln County jail contract nears expiration as records on inmate suicide stay under wraps
item.description:
CARRIZOZO — Lincoln County's contract with the private company that runs its jail expires in less than four months. Records released to AlamogordoTownNews.org show the county pays the operator about $5.45 million a year. But the county has not released records about an inmate suicide at the facility or about staffing levels there, and its attorney says the next update on the request won't come until mid-December.

Correctional Solutions Group LLC (CSG), based in Tyler, Texas, has run the Lincoln County Detention Center under an agreement signed Jan. 28, 2020. That agreement set a five-year initial term with up to four two-year renewals. On Nov. 19, 2024, County Commission Chairman Todd F. Proctor and CSG Chief Operating Officer David L. Stanfield signed the first renewal. It extends the contract from Jan. 28, 2025, through Jan. 27, 2027. The renewal also references a second amendment dated June 11, 2024, which was not among the documents released.

What the county pays

A CSG budget dated Oct. 30, 2024, which the county provided as the cost breakdown for the renewal, sets the county's monthly payment at $454,541.88. That figure includes New Mexico's 7.2% gross receipts tax and comes to $5,454,502.59 a year.

Payroll accounts for about $2.55 million of that. Once taxes, insurance and benefits are added, total staff compensation comes to about $3.22 million. The largest cost outside payroll is general liability insurance at $528,000 a year, followed by food service at $163,200.

The budget sets aside about $70,000 a year for a contract physician, $7,800 for over-the-counter medication and $6,300 for general medical supplies. A line for mental health tele-psychiatry shows no money budgeted. A note beside it is cut off in the released copy, and it cannot be determined from the document whether that service is funded elsewhere. Employee training is budgeted at $8,532 a year and staff incentives at $8,400.

The spreadsheet projects CSG will earn about $773,500 a year before an insurance-related deduction and about $698,700 after it. It lists monthly margins between roughly 11% and 16%. Notations on the budget indicate some costs, including the gross receipts tax and liability insurance, are subject to negotiation or periodic "true-up" adjustments.

A 2020 amendment shows the jail also holds inmates for the federal Bureau of Indian Affairs. Because of that, the contract must comply with the federal Service Contract Act, which requires federal prevailing wages and paid sick leave for the jail's workers.

Records request

KALHRadio.org and AlamogordoTownNews.org a request under the New Mexico Inspection of Public Records Act (IPRA) seeking records on the  suicide of an inmate at the jail in 2026, staffing and overtime, video footage, communications from medical staff, and the contract renewal.

In an incorrectly dated April 2, 2026, response, Ruidoso attorney Alexandra J. Bobbit, answering on the county's behalf, said many of those records would not be released while the matter is under investigation. The letter cites NMSA 1978 Section 14-2-1.2. The records withheld on that basis include:

• incident reports and investigation files

• the names of staff who responded

• the medical examiner's report

• the inmate's medical and mental health records

• video footage

• all communications from healthcare staff to jail or county officials in the 90 days before the incident

The letter confirmed that surveillance cameras were working in the cell or area where the death occurred. It said the recordings are in CSG's possession and declined to say who else has them.

A second group of records was described only as "currently with CSG," with more time needed to respond. That group includes:

• staffing rosters and shift records for the night of the death

• facility safety inspections for the prior 90 days

• records on cell visibility and window design

• three years of staffing, overtime and turnover data

• any internal communications raising concerns about understaffing or staff fatigue

On the contract, the county released the 2020 amendment, the 2024 renewal and the budget. It pointed to meeting minutes on the county website and said no renewal proposals or counterproposals have been found so far.

The letter says the request remains open and promises an update by Dec. 15, 2026. That is more than eight months after the response and about six weeks before the jail contract expires. IPRA generally requires public bodies to produce records within 15 days. The law allows more time when a request is broad or burdensome.

Our counsel believes that parts of the request are being stonewalled and the response does not meet statutory requirements. 

KALHRadio.org and AlamogordoTownNews.org challenges county's delay

On September 29th we sent a written demand to the county's attorney and records custodian. It asks the county to release, at a minimum, the staffing, overtime, inspection and cell-visibility records that the county described as "with CSG," along with internal communications about understaffing and fatigue.

The letter argues that records CSG holds while running the jail are county public records under IPRA. It cites New Mexico Court of Appeals rulings holding that a private company performing a government function under contract is subject to the law, including a 2020 case involving a private prison health care contractor.

The letter also argues that the county missed IPRA's deadlines. Under the law, a public body must produce records within 15 days or notify the requester within that window that it needs more time for a broad request. The county's first response came in late September, more than 15 days after our August request, and did not claim the request was too broad.

The letter asks the county to:

• produce the staffing records for the night of the death and the 90 days of inspection logs within 10 days

• begin releasing the remaining records on a set schedule

• give a formal written explanation, with legal grounds, for anything it withholds

• confirm that CSG has been told to preserve all related records, including video

It notes that the law allows a requester to go to court, where the public body can be ordered to pay costs, attorney fees and damages.

Why the records matter

The records at issue go to how the county's jail is run, and they are being sought during an unusually troubled stretch for the facility. In recent months, an inmate escaped as reported by the news outlet and other major media; an inmate died by suicide in August prompting the release request, another inmate attempted suicide in September, and the  jail's health care provider was released under questionable circumstances.  Staffing rosters, inspection logs, overtime data and staff communications are among the few ways the public can check whether those events are connected to how the jail is staffed and managed.

The county pays CSG about $5.45 million a year in public money, and the current contract expires Jan. 27, 2027. Commissioners will soon decide whether to renew it, and residents may not see these records before that decision unless the county releases them sooner. Stay tuned; citizens and taxpayers deserve transparency and open access to government information and functions.

item.title: In Memory of John Gregory Greene
item.description:
John Gregory Greene, beloved father, partner, and friend, passed away tragically on September 21, 2026. He was born on June 18, 1983, in Fredericksburg, Texas to Alan and Tina Greene.

John is survived and remembered by his three children, Randi, Graham, and Skoodee Greene, and his beloved partner, Randa. He was the oldest brother to 5 siblings, as well as an uncle, nephew, cousin, and godfather.

John had a profound love for shiny things and the simple life. He enjoyed working with his sons and watching them grow. John loved to ride in the Gator with his dog chief and travel in his bus. He was always hunting down new restaurants with his daughter in search of a good ribeye. He never missed an opportunity and treated every day as if it were a holiday.

John was well traveled and well versed in the ways of life. Wise beyond his years, kind, stoic, and loving, were all of the ways we knew him.

John passed far too soon leaving behind family, friends, and people who loved him deeply. His soul is eternal in love and faith.

Forever young.

The Memorial Service for John Greene will be held at 3:00 pm, Tuesday, September 29, 2026, at Alamogordo Funeral Home with Pastor Justin Crispen officiating.

item.title: Court officials say they didn't know ICE agents were at Otero County courthouse; county has yet to respond
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — Officials with the Twelfth Judicial District say they had no advance knowledge that federal immigration agents were on courthouse grounds on Sept. 22, when masked men who identified themselves as ICE agents detained a man moments after a judge dismissed the criminal case against him.

The man's name has not been released.

Audrey Hukari, chief clerk and court executive officer for the Twelfth Judicial District and Magistrate Courts, responded to a request for comment sent Sunday to District Judge Angie Schneider and the court clerk's office. Hukari said the court "can not comment on specific cases," but that court staff "were not aware of federal immigration agents being present on September 22nd."

Hukari also said there was no communication about the case "outside of normal business practices related to the conclusion of any court case." She did not say what those practices include.

Arrest took place in county-owned lot, court says

According to Hukari, the detention happened in the courthouse parking lot, which is owned by Otero County, not the court. She said the lot is shared by several government entities, including the district court, and serves both the public and court staff.

An emailed request for comment to the Otero County CEO, asking about the county's policy on immigration enforcement on county property and whether the county was aware of the detention, has not received a response as of publication.

The parking lot detail matters because of the statewide rules that govern courthouse access. Hukari pointed to a New Mexico Supreme Court order, No. S-1-AO-2025-00023, which she said all judicial districts follow.

The order took effect Nov. 17, 2025, and applies to "all courthouses and buildings owned or occupied by the New Mexico Judicial Branch." The policy does not specifically address parking lots or other grounds outside court buildings.

What the statewide policy says

The Supreme Court policy does not prohibit immigration arrests at courthouses. It requires any on-duty law enforcement officer from an outside agency, whether local, state, tribal or federal, to present a badge and official credentials to on-site courthouse security immediately upon entering. It also requires any arrest or detention inside a courthouse to be carried out in a way that does not interfere with court proceedings.

In the order, the justices said courthouses should remain open and accessible to "individuals, families, and businesses," and that people should be able to take part in proceedings free of "harassment or threats to their security or freedom." Violations of the policy can be enforced through each court's contempt powers.

Because the court says the Sept. 22 detention happened outside the building, it is unclear whether the identification requirement or any other part of the policy applied.

Immigration status not tracked

Hukari said the court does not record immigration status. "An individual's immigration status is not tracked as a data point in our case management system," she wrote.

She added that the Twelfth Judicial District is committed to providing access to justice through fair, timely and efficient resolution of all cases within its jurisdiction.

Public defender raised concerns

The incident first came to light through an email from Dayna Louise Jones, District Defender for the 12th Judicial District with the Law Office of the Public Defender, to the district's Criminal Justice Coordinating Council.

Jones wrote that the man, a client of her office, was taken immediately after his case was dismissed. His children, who were with him, described the men as masked and traveling in an unmarked vehicle. Jones wrote that people present told her office the detention "appeared to be coordinated and preplanned with local entities," though she did not name any agency.

Jones cited a 2025 state law meant to keep state agency employees from disclosing a person's immigration status. Separately, the Immigrant Safety Act, House Bill 9, which took effect May 20, bars state and local public bodies from agreements with ICE for civil immigration detention.

"The courthouse should be a safe place for individuals who are seeing their cases through to their resolutions," Jones wrote.

This story will be updated if the county responds.

item.title: Second Inmate Dies by Suicide at Lincoln County Detention Center; 24-Year-Old Was Held for BIA
item.description:
The inmate was reportedly being held on behalf of the federal Bureau of Indian Affairs. The inmate's name and the circumstances of the death have not been released, and county officials have not publicly confirmed the incident. The sources spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly.

The death comes the same day AlamogordoTownNews.org and KALHRadio.org reported that Lincoln County is withholding records about the jail's previous suicide.

Requests for information have been sent to Lincoln County officials, detention center administration and the office of Sheriff Wood. As of publication, none had responded

Records still withheld

The county has not released records about the August suicide or staffing levels at the jail, and its attorney has said the next update on the request won't come until mid-December. Citing an ongoing investigation, the county is withholding incident reports, the medical examiner's report, video footage, and healthcare staff communications to jail or county officials from the 90 days before the death. The county said other records, including staffing rosters for the night of the death, recent safety inspections and records on cell visibility, are held by the jail's private operator.

On Tuesday, this news outlet sent a written demand to the county's attorney and records custodian. It asks the county to release the staffing and inspection records and to confirm that the operator has been told to preserve all related records, including video.

Private operator, public money

Correctional Solutions Group LLC (CSG) of Tyler, Texas, has run the jail since 2020. The county pays CSG about $5.45 million a year, and the current contract expires Jan. 27, 2027.

The budget CSG submitted for the contract renewal sets aside about $70,000 a year for a contract physician. Its line for mental health tele-psychiatry shows no money budgeted, and the document does not show whether that service is funded elsewhere.

Federal ties

Because the jail houses BIA inmates, its contract must comply with the federal Service Contract Act. The death of a BIA detainee may also trigger federal reporting requirements and scrutiny. It is not yet known whether the inmate's tribe has been notified or whether state or federal authorities are investigating.

A costly precedent

The deaths recall the case of Natasha Bloos, whose death led to a $2.4 million settlement this year. Bloos had been moved from the Lincoln County jail to the state women's prison near Grants after earlier suicide attempts. A judge had ordered the move, finding the Lincoln County facility could not give her the medical care or supervision she needed. She died by suicide at the prison about two weeks later. The settlement benefits her three minor children.

Lincoln County commissioners will soon decide whether to renew CSG's contract. This is a developing story, and AlamogordoTownNews.org will update it as officials respond.

item.title: Conflicting Accounts Emerge in Death of 24-Year-Old Lincoln County Inmate; Jail Medical Oversight Questioned
item.description:
CARRIZOZO, N.M. — Accounts of how a 24-year-old inmate died at the Lincoln County Detention Center on Monday, Sept. 28, now conflict. Questions are also growing about who, if anyone, is directing medical care at the jail.

AlamogordoTownNews.org and KALHRadio.org first reported the death as an apparent suicide, based on sources within the jail and the judiciary. Another jail staff member has since given a different account. That staff member says the inmate was a diabetic, was going through alcohol withdrawal, and died in a cell equipped with a camera. The staff member spoke on condition of anonymity with fear of retaliation from the Warden or operating company. .

The cause of death has not been officially determined. The Office of the Medical Investigator typically makes that finding. The inmate, who was reportedly being held on behalf of the federal Bureau of Indian Affairs, has not been identified.

Warden declines comment on death

In a phone interview with Anthony Lucero of the Alamogordo Town News streaming edition on KALHRadio.org, Warden Castleton declined to confirm or discuss the details of the death. The full interview is available on our YouTube page:

“Unfortunately, in situations like this, I’m not allowed to really give information,” the warden said. He explained that such cases go to the Lincoln County Sheriff’s Office for investigation.

Asked about health care at the jail, the warden said, “Our healthcare providers are provided through WSI. It’s a company out of Colorado. … It’s a third-party contract that we have with them.”

What WSI says it does

WSI Healthcare Personnel Inc. describes itself as a staffing company, not a medical provider. According to its website, it places clinicians with facilities on a per diem, temp-to-hire or direct-hire basis. It says it has served communities since 1988.

The company’s own materials also address who is accountable for care. WSI’s website notes that facilities are still responsible for the quality of care even when they outsource staffing.

Staff member disputes warden’s account

A jail staff member employed through WSI echoed that description. The staff member, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said WSI’s role is to supply personnel, not to run the jail’s medical program. “WSI has tried to place a medical provider at the jail, the staff member said, but no one has been willing to take the job given the pay and travel required.”

Asked who the jail’s current provider is, the staff member said, “There isn’t one. There is no medical provider providing medical orders.”

The staff member said the warden is relying on semantics in describing WSI’s role. They said the central question is who, if anyone, is issuing verbal or written orders for inmates’ medical care. For a diabetic inmate, that would include orders for blood glucose checks or insulin. The staff member said WSI’s chief executive is aware that the warden has attributed the jail’s medical care to the company.

AlamogordoTownNews.org has asked the county, the warden, jail operator Correctional Solutions Group, WSI and Sheriff Wood’s office to identify who currently issues medical orders at the facility. As of publication, none had responded but an update is expected on Wednesday. 

Why it matters

Inmates withdrawing from alcohol and inmates with diabetes both typically need medical monitoring under a provider’s orders. Whether any such orders were in place before Monday’s death is among the questions put to county and jail officials.

The death follows months of trouble at the jail. In recent months an inmate escaped, an inmate died by suicide in August, and another inmate attempted suicide in September. Over the same period, members of the jail’s health care provider left under questionable circumstances.

The budget CSG submitted to the county sets aside about $70,000 a year for a contract physician. It lists no funding for mental health tele-psychiatry.

The county is withholding records on the August death, citing an ongoing investigation. Those records include communications from health care staff in the 90 days before that death. The county says its next update on the records request will come in mid-December. On Tuesday, the news outlets sent a written demand to the county seeking faster release.

CSG, based in Tyler, Texas, is paid about $5.45 million a year to run the jail. Its contract expires Jan. 27, 2027, and county commissioners will soon decide whether to renew it.

A costly precedent

The jail’s record on inmate care has been costly before. The case of Natasha Bloos led to a $2.4 million settlement this year. A judge had ordered Bloos moved from the Lincoln County jail to the state women’s prison near Grants after earlier suicide attempts, finding the county facility could not give her the medical care or supervision she needed. She died by suicide at the prison about two weeks later.

item.title: Alamogordo residents press regulators over soaring PNM bills
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — Residents packed a city-hosted town hall to tell state utility regulators that their PNM electric bills doubled, tripled and in some cases topped $1,000 this summer, and to demand a formal investigation and an independent test of the utility's meters.

The New Mexico Public Regulation Commission (PRC) sent Commissioner Greg Nibert, its public advocacy staff, its chief of staff and its public information officer to hear complaints about July and August 2026 bills. Mayor Sharon McDonald opened the session, noting the city itself has no role in PNM billing but wanted to give residents a forum.

PRC advocacy staff told the crowd the problem traces to a shortage of meter readers that led to estimated and delayed bills, and said their review is not finished. "We are not done investigating," one staff attorney said.

PRC advocacy staff said PNM shifted personnel ahead of a planned rollout of smart meters, which will not need to be read in person, and then saw unexpected turnover. That left Alamogordo short of meter readers this summer.

PNM moved readers in from Albuquerque and Santa Fe, which created shortages elsewhere. Staff said the problem started in Otero County but spread across PNM's service territory. They said they have been told readings are now back on schedule.

Customers with usage history received estimated bills based on past consumption. Customers PNM could not estimate for got delayed bills, sometimes covering two months at once. Staff said the delayed bills were one reason for the spikes, "but probably not the only" one.

Staff also said a two-stage rate increase approved by the PRC took effect in summer 2025 and April 2026. They said they did not recognize a 27 percent figure cited by one resident, but conceded the increase "was not adequately communicated" to the community.

On speculation about private equity firm Blackstone, staff noted the firm is seeking to buy PNM but does not own it, and that the sale requires commission approval.

Rebecca Stewart Thorpe spoke for PNM Customers United, a Facebook group she said has nearly 1,100 members. She said the group has no evidence of wrongdoing but wants the PRC to open a formal investigation into July and August billing. The group also asked for preserved meter data, refunds where errors are found and a halt to disconnections during disputes.

Thorpe pointed to Otero County Electric Cooperative customers, who faced the same heat without the same billing complaints.

Many speakers said a missed meter reading led to a two-month bill that pushed their usage into higher-priced tiers. Terry Carroll held up a chart showing one bill more than three times his usual amount. He said he paid $1,000 of a bill over $1,700 and refused to pay the rest.

Kelly and James Metcalf, a one-income family with five children, received a $1,949.26 bill on Sept. 17 for 62 days. The same period last year cost about $506, they said. James Metcalf later asked whether customers will be refunded.

Others described bills rising even after they cut usage. Johnny Martin, 74, said he spent $12,000 on a new air conditioner and upgraded appliances, yet has had four straight bills over $400. He said he waited on hold for 30 minutes and never reached anyone.

Frank Guerrero, 73, said his bill jumped from about $70 to $172. He spoke for a friend caring for his wife, who is dying of cancer, and received a $700 bill.

A couple who live where Tularosa Creek meets Highway 54 said PNM crews replacing poles shut off their solar system and never switched it back on. Their usual $16 bill became $256.

Tina Martinez, a board member at Love INC, said the charity runs PNM's Good Neighbor assistance program locally. It can help only 15 households a month, at $175 each, she said, while PNM's local office keeps sending people there.

Several residents, including Paul Sanchez, called for an independent company to test a large sample of meters. Some described new digital meters that flash, go blank or show all eights.

Not everyone was hit. Tanya Burns and Greg Gutierrez said their own bills were normal while neighbors' soared. Burns also criticized state Rep. John Block, who attended, as "political theatrics" with the Nov. 3 election weeks away.

Mark Hayden of the New Mexico Department of Justice, representing Attorney General Raúl Torrez, said the office has received about 30 complaints. He said the department met with PNM and will stay involved until the billing issues are resolved.

PRC staff said PNM has told them it suspended disconnections and late fees for affected customers and is offering payment arrangements. Staff asked anyone who receives a disconnection threat to report it to the PRC.

PNM billing staff and meter specialists worked with residents at a table in the back of the room during the meeting.

Customers who cannot resolve a bill with PNM can file an informal complaint with the PRC's customer relations division, then a formal complaint if that fails. The PRC can be reached through its website, by phone at 1-888-427-5772, or by mail at 142 W. Palace Ave., Santa Fe.

Staff said estimated bills may still be corrected on later statements. Residents can also comment at the commission's open meetings, including one planned in Las Cruces in October. The coverage continues by Alamogordo Town News and KALHRadio.org

item.title: Independent Voters on the Rise in New Mexico
item.description:
More New Mexicans are choosing not to pick a party, and one local researcher says political parties ignore that shift at their own risk.

In a conversation with Anthony, Stephanie, an accountant and researcher, laid out the numbers behind the growth of independent and decline-to-state (DTS) voters. She connected the trend to a decades-old political science idea known as partisan realignment.

Nationally, Stephanie pointed to a Gallup poll finding that a record 45% of Americans identified as independent in 2025. Republicans and Democrats each drew 27%.

New Mexico is seeing the same pattern. Bernalillo County has the most independent and DTS voters in raw numbers. By share of registered voters, Doña Ana County leads at 31%, with Otero County close behind at 30%.

Curious about the trend, Stephanie began asking people why they registered as independents. Several answers stood out. Some said it makes it easier to keep friendships intact. Others said they don't want to explain their vote to anyone, or be labeled by either side.

Those answers fit partisan realignment, she said: voters grow less attached to a party even while holding strong political views.

"Basically, more Americans are saying, 'Don't define my politics for me,'" Stephanie said. "I'll decide issue by issue and candidate by candidate."

New Mexico made the DTS path more appealing with Senate Bill 16, passed in 2025. The law lets DTS voters choose a party's primary ballot without changing their registration.

Stephanie expects the change to draw even more voters to register DTS. She said the first election after the bill passed added 10% more votes to the primary. "That's one in ten," she said, calling it a very significant number for New Mexico.

For years, Stephanie said, parties have grown comfortable expecting votes based on party alone. As the independent population grows, more of those votes may have to be earned on the candidate, the policy and the issue.

She has seen what happens when a party misses that chance. She once introduced an intern to a number of elected officials. When a party chair asked his affiliation and he answered DTS, the chair replied, "I can't help you then."

"What a missed opportunity," Stephanie said. The intern was a young person interested in government, she noted, and instead of being asked what mattered to him, he was dismissed for not choosing a party.

With the midterms ahead, Stephanie said it will be worth watching how independent voters shape the 2026 results and what that signals for 2028.

For anyone not yet registered, she noted it isn't too late. New Mexico lets eligible voters register and vote on the same day during early voting at participating locations, or on Election Day.

item.title: In Loving Memory of Joseph “Jody” Mancillas
item.description:
Joseph “Jody” Mancillas, age 55, passed away peacefully on September 18, 2026. He leaves behind a legacy of warmth, kindness, and deeply cherished memories with everyone who had the privilege of knowing him.

One of Jody's greatest accomplishments was his dedicated career working at The Lodge at Cloudcroft for 35 years. It was truly his pride and joy, a place where he built lasting connections and left an undeniable impact through his decades of hard work and commitment.

Jody was a devoted son, brother, and friend who saw the world through a lens of appreciation and joy. In his younger years, he was happiest out on the court, playing basketball alongside his good friends. He loved bowling with his friends; he always brought a spirited energy to the lanes and thoroughly enjoyed the fun of a friendly competition. His love for local athletics continued throughout his life, and he always thoroughly enjoyed playing in local golf scrambles as well as dedicating his time line judging at high school volleyball tournaments.

Jody thoroughly enjoyed his extensive collection of music and movies, and he spent countless hours sharing his talent for baking, creating delicious desserts for both the staff and guests at The Lodge as well as for his beloved family and friends. He also held a deep, lifelong love for trains, and one of his favorite simple pleasures was listening to the train pass by.

Above all, Jody spent many hours on his photography, which was truly the biggest part of his life outside of work. He spent his happiest days hiking through nature, finding hidden beauty in everything around him and capturing it to share with the world. He also enjoyed memorable nights playing cards with the Turner family. Even during his illness, Jody brought people together, sharing lots of laughter, and he absolutely loved playing Farkle.

Known for his generous heart, he brought steady comfort and joy to those around him. His presence will be profoundly missed, but his memory will live on forever in the hearts of those he loved so dearly.

He is survived by his beloved mother, Sherry Crosson (husband Tim), and his brother, Jonathan Mancillas, along with a large, loving family of aunts, uncles, and cousins who will carry his strength and laughter forward. He is preceded in death by his father, Joseph L. Mancillas; his grandparents, Lucas and Angelita Mancillas; and his grandmother, Ruth A. Williams.

item.title: Tularosa Trustees Delay Employee Raises Until Finance Director Can Attend
item.description:
TULAROSA, N.M. — The Tularosa Board of Trustees put off votes on a slate of village employee raises at a special meeting this week, after trustees said they could not weigh the budget impact without the village finance director in the room.

The board agreed to reconvene Monday at 6 p.m., when the mayor said the finance director would attend with figures. No raises were approved.

During public comment, Vivian Lewis told trustees she had learned of the special meeting only that Monday. She said a raise the municipal judge requested for her at earlier budget hearings was already written into the court's budget, which took effect July 1, but she had not received it.

The village's legal adviser, identified at the meeting as Nan, said a raise inside an approved budget does not need a new vote. If the employee was told the raise would start with the new fiscal year, she said, the employee is entitled to it from that date.

Asked whether the roughly $2-an-hour difference owed since July 1 should come as a supplemental check, the adviser deferred to the finance officer, saying a lump sum or an adjusted paycheck would both work.

The raises followed employee performance evaluations submitted by department heads. The police chief told trustees she had turned in her evaluations early and asked for raises, but they were left out of her department's budget. Police spending makes up more than half the village budget, she said, and "runs a little tight."

The mayor said the raises would come from each department's own budget, not the general fund. Several trustees pushed back, saying the raises were never budgeted and that they had raised the issue before the budget was adopted.

One trustee estimated that approving every raise on the agenda would add about $55,000, against roughly $170,000 the village has available. "We're not against giving raises," the trustee said, but the board needs to know where the money comes from.

Another trustee noted that some line items had already reached 157% of their budget two months into the fiscal year. He said he had asked at the prior meeting for the finance director, Valerie, to attend and had been assured she would. The mayor said she was unavailable.

The legal adviser told the board it first had to make a policy call: whether the raises would be paid from the general fund or from department budgets. Without the finance director, she said, that question was hard to answer.

Raises that fit inside a department's existing budget could proceed without further action, she said. Raises that don't would require a budget adjustment resolution once approved.

The mayor proposed setting aside the police chief's requests and voting on departments that could cover their own raises, including the utility supervisor, the senior center director and Clerk Garcia's three requests. But the clerk said she was willing to wait "because I don't think it's fair for everybody else." The board then agreed to hold all the raises until Monday.

With time left before adjourning, a trustee raised questions about specific public works wages. She said two employees, Nathan and Brett, took on new duties at the water plant without a wage change. She suggested extra pay for Brett, the department's only backup commercial driver's license holder, so the trash route can run when the regular driver is out.

Staff said Brett already earns trash-truck-driver pay for hours he drives, but nothing extra for holding the CDL. The adviser noted that such pay is the supervisor's call. The supervisor also confirmed an error in one employee's proposed raise, which will be corrected to $2, and said she would like to give part-time worker Carlos a $2 raise after a strong evaluation.

The utility supervisor reported the village reservoir at 36.5 feet as of that morning. The village is not drawing from it because of recent rain.

The board meets again Monday at 6 p.m. to take up the raises.

item.title: Otero Arts Packs October with Photography, Music, Film and Free Workshops
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — Otero Arts has filled its October calendar with a month-long photography exhibit, a baroque chamber concert, an author reading, a lecture on ancient Egypt, a documentary screening and free hands-on workshops, nearly all of them at the Otero Artspace at 12th and Indiana.

The all-volunteer nonprofit, now led by newly elected Board President Kim Melton, opens the month on Thursday, Oct. 1, and keeps something on the schedule almost every week through Oct. 28.

Nature photographer and Otero Arts member Stan Ford headlines the month with a solo show. An opening reception runs Friday, Oct. 2, from 5 to 7 p.m. After that, the exhibit is free and open Thursday through Sunday, 1 to 4 p.m., until it closes Oct. 24.

Ford spent this past May as artist-in-residence at Valles Caldera National Preserve, the third time the National Park Service has chosen him to teach photography at one of its parks. His workshops usually focus on night photography, and this year's class caught a rare sight. Ford said the class was fortunate to see the Northern Lights. Images from the park, including a cabin at sunrise and the aurora over the caldera, are part of the show.

Ford will be at the Artspace on Friday, Oct. 9, from 1 to 4 p.m. to meet members and fellow photographers.

The monthly Free Art Workshop on Saturday, Oct. 10, teaches Imani paper pumpkins with instructor Pennie Espiritu. Reserve a spot by emailing mariaaragon64@gmail.com or signing up at oteroarts.org. The workshop is funded by Thrive! of Southern New Mexico. Espiritu will also preview the craft at the Oct. 1 Meet and Greet.

For more serious painters, Anita Louise West leads a three-day Plein Air Painting Workshop Oct. 13–15, painting historic villages and local landscapes. The cost is $200, and the class is limited to 10 students. A few spaces remain; tickets are at oteroarts.org, and questions go to oteroartsinc@gmail.com.

Reading Series, Friday, Oct. 16, 6 p.m. Jennifer Givhan, a Mexican-American and Indigenous poet and novelist from the Desert Southwest, reads at the Artspace. Givhan has received fellowships from the NEA and PEN/Rosenthal Emerging Voices and won the Southwest Book Award. She has written seven poetry collections and five novels, most recently The Sleeping Sisters.

Cruzando Fronteras, Saturday, Oct. 17, 7 p.m. The Baroque Chamber Ensemble performs music of Bach, Vivaldi, Handel and Scarlatti. Players include Stephen Redfield and Carla Moore on baroque violins, Katie Rietman on baroque cello, Charlotte Mattax Moersch on harpsichord and Gerard Gibbs on recorder. Tickets are $25 at oteroarts.org.

JRI Lecture, Tuesday, Oct. 20, 6 p.m. In the monthly partnership with the Jornada Research Institute, Dave Greenwald presents "Historic Cairo and Ancient Nile Explorations." He previews the sites his tour group will visit this fall, including the Great Pyramids, the inside of the Pyramid of Khufu, the Sphinx and the wider Giza Necropolis.

Film Series, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 5:30 p.m. The documentary The Curious World of Hieronymus Bosch gathers the medieval painter's masterpieces from around the world in his Dutch hometown. Admission is free; donations are welcome.

The month starts with the First Thursdays Meet and Greet on Oct. 1, 10 to 11:30 a.m., with coffee, conversation and Espiritu's paper pumpkin demo. Belly dance classes begin Thursday, Oct. 8, at 5:30 p.m. and continue weekly; contact Claudia Powell at claudia@tularosa.net. The Otero Arts board meets Tuesday, Oct. 13, at 1:30 p.m., and members are welcome.

Elsewhere in the area, Alamogordo MainStreet hosts "Heroes on Mainstreet" Oct. 2, 4 to 8 p.m., on the 900 block of New York Avenue

The Flickinger Center screens the Banff Mountain Film Festival Oct. 9 and stages the Children's Music Theater's "Frozen" Oct. 16–18 and 23–24.

Thrive in Southern New Mexico, an Otero Arts grant provider, holds its Corks & Shells Wine & Pistachio Festival Oct. 17 at Alameda Park. 

The Cloudcroft Art Society's Holiday Show opens Oct. 3, 11 a.m. to 3 p.m.

The Otero Artspace is at 1118 Indiana Ave. in Alamogordo. For details, visit oteroarts.org, call 575-446-3880 or email oteroartsinc@gmail.com.

item.title: Commentary: Same Pattern, Same Silence: Potential Sexual Harassment at Alamogordo City Hall Demands Answers
item.description:
Alamogordo NM Commentary- Over the past 60 days, several city employees have come to us with the same concern: City Hall has become a workplace where comments about appearance are tolerated, assignments seem to follow favor rather than merit, and people are afraid to speak up. These are not new problems here. That is exactly why they deserve answers now.

I am not writing to accuse any individual of a crime. I am writing because what employees describe, if accurate, falls short of the city's own policies and could expose taxpayers to real legal liability.

A double standard on workplace conduct

Employees describe a senior official who has publicly criticized others for using familiar, family-style terms with coworkers, while themself commenting openly on an employee's looks and body. In one instance, employees say the department leader joked that “he should pose for a calendar and could fill all twelve months.” “He could be my Santa January thru December.” 

Swap the genders and few would hesitate to call that inappropriate. Comments about a subordinate's physical appearance are exactly what the city's harassment training warns against. When they come from leadership, they set the tone for everyone below. They also tell employees which rules are enforced, and for whom.

What innuendo costs a workplace

A "joke" about a coworker's body is never only a joke. The EEOC's bipartisan Select Task Force on harassment found that harassment affects all workers, not just the target, and that its true cost includes lost productivity, higher turnover, and reputational harm. The task force's co-chairs testified that lost productivity often shows up as quiet disengagement, and that a bad reputation drives away potential new hires.

The task force also found that harassment too often goes unreported, because people fear being disbelieved, blamed, or punished. In a city government where everyone knows everyone, that fear is magnified. When leaders make suggestive comments in front of staff, every employee learns that appearance is being noticed and graded. Those who object learn to stay quiet, and the best of them start looking for other jobs.

The perception of favoritism

Employees also describe projects being pulled from one manager and handed to another, the same one singled out for comments on his appearance, with no clear explanation. Some department directors are reportedly seen frequently with the city manager outside work, and staff say those directors appear to receive preferential treatment.

Perception matters in public service. Even if every decision has a sound reason, employees who cannot see that reason will fill the gap themselves. That erodes trust, morale, and the city's ability to keep good people.

Meanwhile, some targeted employees have been placed on paid administrative leave. Coworkers worry the pattern targets people who "don't fit the image" leadership wants. Paid leave costs taxpayers twice: once for the person on leave, and again for the work left undone. The public deserves to know the criteria being used.

We have been here before

In 2023, the city added sexual harassment content to commission training after a departing employee raised concerns in an exit interview. Her concern, as it was relayed, was whether appearance affected how some commissioners treated staff.

That same year, the city hired outside counsel to independently investigate the conduct of its commissioners. One sitting commissioner was named in that investigation and again in a second outside investigation in 2025. The December 2023 report found credible evidence that commissioners broke the city's Code of Conduct by going around the city manager to pressure employees.

The same report recorded a former city attorney's exit-interview allegation that a commissioner had engaged in sexual harassment. It found the Code of Conduct gave no clear guidance on handling that complaint, and nothing indicates the allegation was ever investigated. Excerpts of both reports became public only this month, after persistent records requests by Alamogordo Town News. 

Each episode was handled quietly and then forgotten. Employees now see a familiar pattern taking shape, and they have little faith it will be handled differently.

This city has watched leadership scandals play out before, with residents left to absorb the cost.

What this has already cost taxpayers

Alamogordo's habit of settling quietly is well documented:

• About a decade ago, the city agreed to pay $137,500 to its former personnel manager. She alleged she was demoted and fired after supporting a coworker she believed was being treated unfairly.

That coworker, a former public safety lieutenant, settled separately for $250,000.

• In 2023, the city manager left under a retirement and settlement agreement after accusing commissioners of interfering with staff. The outside investigator found his core allegations credible.

• In 2025, a second outside report found the search for a permanent city manager had been "tainted." It warned that passing over the top-scoring candidate, the only woman in the pool, could support a discrimination claim.

• In April 2026, after closed sessions, the commission voted 4–3 to accept a settlement tied to that candidate's EEOC complaint. The terms were not disclosed in open session.

The two figures made public total $387,500 in net pay closer to a half million in total. The rest remain undisclosed, along with the cost of repeated recruitments and outside legal work.

Title VII applies at City Hall

Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 covers employers with 15 or more employees, and that includes city governments. Under it, sexual harassment is a form of illegal sex discrimination. It covers unwelcome verbal conduct of a sexual nature that creates an intimidating, hostile, or offensive work environment, or that interferes with someone's work.

Three points matter here. The person harassed does not have to be the opposite sex of the harasser, so comments by a woman about a man count the same. No one has to be fired or demoted for harassment to be unlawful. And it is separately illegal to retaliate against anyone who complains or cooperates with an investigation.

When a city loses or settles these claims, the bill does not go to the officials involved. It goes to the city's budget and its insurance pool, which means it goes to residents. New Mexico's Human Rights Act adds state-level exposure on top of the federal law.

What the city should do now

The commission can get ahead of this before the next complaint becomes the next settlement:

• Commission an independent review of the current workplace complaints, conducted by an outside HR firm or attorney who reports to the full commission, not the city manager.

• Release the findings of both outside investigation reports in full, with only legally required redactions, and explain what was done about the harassment allegation.

• Disclose the total amount paid in employee settlements over the past ten years.

• Publish the criteria used to place employees on paid administrative leave, and report how many are on leave today and at what cost.

• Require refresher harassment training for all elected officials and senior staff, with attendance made public.

Alamogordo is better than this

This city runs on people who show up: the crews who keep the water running, the clerks who answer every call, the officers and firefighters who work every holiday. They deserve leaders who treat them as professionals, not as gossip or as pin-ups. Most of our elected officials and directors know that, and many have said so on the record.

But respect does not enforce itself. Our charter leaves commissioners to police one another, and the record shows how rarely that happens, how ineffective and how it further supports the good ole boy narrative. Accountability will come only if residents ask for it, out loud and in person.

The next regular commission meeting is Tuesday, Oct. 13, at 6:30 p.m. Come to public comment. Ask for the reports, the settlement totals, and an independent review. Employees should not have to choose between their careers and a respectful workplace, and residents should not keep learning the truth only after the check clears.
